name: Holy Basil (Tulsi) Steady Spirit Tincture
description: Tulsi, the 'Incomparable One', is planted in courtyards across India as a living shrine to the goddess Tulsi and to Vishnu. This bright, clove-scented tincture is a folk adaptogen for the long, grinding kind of stress that wears down body and spirit alike.

ingredients.item: Holy Basil leaves and flowering tops, dried

steps: Cleanse a clean, dry pint (500 ml) glass jar with a pass of incense smoke or a whispered blessing, and hold your intention as you work.
Place the dried herbs in the jar, filling it about one-third to one-half full (roughly 1:5 weight-to-volume: 1 part dried herb by weight to 5 parts liquid by volume).

Pour the 80-100 proof (40-50%) vodka or brandy over the herbs until fully covered by at least 1 inch (2.5 cm); poke out air bubbles with a chopstick and top up over the first days if the plant matter swells.
Cap tightly (line metal lids with baking parchment), label with herbs, menstruum and date, and shake while speaking the chant.
Store in a cool, dark cupboard for 4-6 weeks, shaking daily; traditionally begin on the new moon and strain on the full moon a cycle and a half later.
Strain through a cheesecloth-lined strainer, squeezing the marc (spent herbs) firmly to release every drop, then return the herbs to the earth with thanks.
Bottle in amber dropper bottles and label with name, herbs, alcohol %, date made and dose. Stored cool and dark, alcohol tinctures keep for several years.
howToUse: Traditional adult dose: 30-60 drops (1.5-3 ml) in a little water or tea, 2-3 times daily, best taken over several weeks for long-standing stress. Pairs well with a morning cup of tulsi tea.
chant: Sacred basil, holy flame, steady my spirit, still my frame. Through every trial, every test, grant me balance, grant me rest.
intention: I meet the demands of my life with a steady, sacred calm.
timing: New moon on a Thursday or Sunday; strain at the full moon.
caution: Holy basil may lower blood sugar and slow blood clotting; take care with diabetes medication or blood thinners and stop 2 weeks before surgery. Animal studies suggest it may reduce fertility, so avoid it when trying to conceive, in pregnancy and while breastfeeding. Lemon balm may affect thyroid medication and add to sedatives. Alcohol-based: not for pregnancy, breastfeeding, children, anyone in recovery from alcohol use or avoiding alcohol, or people with liver disease, and never take it with disulfiram (Antabuse), metronidazole or tinidazole (or within 3 days of the last dose), or alongside sedatives, opioids or other medicines that react with alcohol. Stirring drops into hot water drives off only part of the alcohol, so it is never alcohol-free; a glycerite (3 parts food-grade glycerin to 1 part water) or vinegar version is the alcohol-free alternative. Traditional folk use only, not a substitute for medical care; consult a healthcare provider before use, especially if you take medication or have a health condition.
bestTime: Late summer, Lughnasadh to Mabon (Aug–Sep), when tulsi flowers are at their most fragrant
interactions: May add to diabetes medicines, blood thinners and antiplatelet drugs; lemon balm may add to sedatives and affect thyroid medication.
pets: Keep away from pets: alcohol tinctures are poisonous to dogs and especially cats.

name: Ashwagandha Root Grounding Tincture
description: Ashwagandha's name means 'smell of the horse', said to grant the strength and stamina of a stallion. A deep, earthy root of Ayurvedic tradition, it is tinctured by hedge-witches who feel scattered, depleted and wired-but-tired.

ingredients.item: Ashwagandha root, dried, cut and sifted

steps: Cleanse a clean, dry pint (500 ml) glass jar with a pass of incense smoke or a whispered blessing, and hold your intention as you work.
Place the chopped dried root and cinnamon in the jar at a 1:5 weight-to-volume ratio (about 55 g root to 275-300 ml liquid); roots swell, so the jar should be no more than one-third full.

Pour the 100 proof (50%) brandy or vodka over the herbs until fully covered by at least 1 inch (2.5 cm); poke out air bubbles with a chopstick and top up over the first days if the plant matter swells.
Cap tightly (line metal lids with baking parchment), label with herbs, menstruum and date, and shake while speaking the chant.
Store in a cool, dark cupboard for 4-6 weeks, shaking daily; begin on the dark or new moon to plant the root's strength, and strain on the full moon.
Strain through a cheesecloth-lined strainer, squeezing the marc (spent herbs) firmly to release every drop, then return the herbs to the earth with thanks.
Bottle in amber dropper bottles and label with name, herbs, alcohol %, date made and dose. Stored cool and dark, alcohol tinctures keep for several years.
howToUse: Traditional adult dose: 30-60 drops (1.5-3 ml) in warm milk, plant milk or water once or twice daily, often in the evening. Folk practice is to take it steadily for 4-8 weeks, then pause.
chant: Root of horse and root of stone, ground me deep and make me whole. Strength to stand and calm to stay, steady I walk upon my way.
intention: I am rooted, resilient and restored.
timing: Dark or new moon on a Saturday; strain at the full moon.
caution: Ashwagandha is a nightshade-family plant: avoid with nightshade allergy. Avoid in pregnancy (traditionally considered able to bring on miscarriage) and breastfeeding. It may affect thyroid hormone levels, blood sugar, blood pressure and immune activity; avoid with hyperthyroidism, autoimmune conditions, or alongside thyroid, diabetes, blood pressure, immunosuppressant sedative or anti-seizure medication unless advised, and with hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (it may raise testosterone). Rare cases of liver injury have been reported; stop if you notice yellowing skin, dark urine or abdominal pain. Long-term safety is not established; take breaks and do not use for more than 3 months at a time. Alcohol-based: not for pregnancy, breastfeeding, children, anyone in recovery from alcohol use or avoiding alcohol, or people with liver disease, and never take it with disulfiram (Antabuse), metronidazole or tinidazole (or within 3 days of the last dose), or alongside sedatives, opioids or other medicines that react with alcohol. Stirring drops into hot water drives off only part of the alcohol, so it is never alcohol-free; a glycerite (3 parts food-grade glycerin to 1 part water) or vinegar version is the alcohol-free alternative. Traditional folk use only, not a substitute for medical care; consult a healthcare provider before use, especially if you take medication or have a health condition.
bestTime: Autumn, Mabon to Samhain (Sep–Oct), when roots are harvested and energy turns inward
interactions: May interact with thyroid hormone, diabetes, blood pressure, immunosuppressant, sedative (including benzodiazepine) and anti-seizure medicines.
pets: Keep away from pets: alcohol tinctures are poisonous to dogs and especially cats.

name: Milk Thistle Seed Liver Guardian Tincture
description: Legend says the white veins on milk thistle's leaves were made by drops of the Virgin Mary's milk, and the seeds have been the herbalist's liver remedy since Dioscorides. A protective, slightly nutty tincture for the hard-working organ of cleansing.

ingredients.item: Milk Thistle seeds, freshly cracked or coarsely ground
Vodka, 120 proof (60% alcohol), or half 190 proof grain alcohol and half water

steps: Cleanse a clean, dry pint (500 ml) glass jar with a pass of incense smoke or a whispered blessing, and hold your intention as you work.
Crack the hard seeds in a coffee grinder or mortar just before use (whole seeds give up little), then place them with the dandelion root in the jar at roughly 1:5 weight-to-volume.
Pour the 60% alcohol over the herbs until fully covered by at least 1 inch (2.5 cm); poke out air bubbles with a chopstick and top up over the first days if the plant matter swells.
Cap tightly (line metal lids with baking parchment), label with herbs, menstruum and date, and shake while speaking the chant.
Store in a cool, dark cupboard for 4-6 weeks, shaking daily; traditionally begin just after the full moon and strain at the dark moon a cycle and a half later.
Strain through a cheesecloth-lined strainer, squeezing the marc (spent herbs) firmly to release every drop, then return the herbs to the earth with thanks.
Bottle in amber dropper bottles and label with name, herbs, alcohol %, date made and dose. Stored cool and dark, alcohol tinctures keep for several years.
howToUse: Traditional adult dose: 40-60 drops (2-3 ml) in water 2-3 times daily before meals, over several weeks. Many herbalists also simply eat 1 tsp of the freshly ground seed on food.
chant: Thistle white with mother's milk, guard my liver, smooth as silk. Cleanse the old and clear the way, strength renewed with every day.
intention: I cleanse and protect the body that carries me.
timing: Waning moon on a Saturday; strain at the dark moon.
caution: Avoid with allergy to the daisy family (ragweed, chrysanthemum, marigold). May lower blood sugar and can affect how the liver processes some drugs; take care with diabetes medication and other prescriptions. Not a treatment for liver disease, hepatitis or alcohol damage, which need medical care, and people with liver disease should avoid the alcohol in this preparation. Avoid with hormone-sensitive conditions unless advised. Milk thistle is poorly extracted by glycerin, so if you need it alcohol-free, eat the ground seed instead. Alcohol-based: not for pregnancy, breastfeeding, children, anyone in recovery from alcohol use or avoiding alcohol, or people with liver disease, and never take it with disulfiram (Antabuse), metronidazole or tinidazole (or within 3 days of the last dose), or alongside sedatives, opioids or other medicines that react with alcohol. Stirring drops into hot water drives off only part of the alcohol, so it is never alcohol-free; a glycerite (3 parts food-grade glycerin to 1 part water) or vinegar version is the alcohol-free alternative. Traditional folk use only, not a substitute for medical care; consult a healthcare provider before use, especially if you take medication or have a health condition.
bestTime: Late summer to early autumn (Aug–Sep), when the thistle heads release their silky seed
interactions: May lower blood sugar (diabetes medicines) and may affect drugs processed by liver enzymes (CYP2C9, CYP3A4), such as warfarin; discuss with your pharmacist.
pets: Keep away from pets: alcohol tinctures are poisonous to dogs and especially cats.

name: Golden Sun Turmeric & Ginger Joint Tincture
description: Turmeric, the golden spice of weddings and blessings across South Asia, joins fiery ginger and a pinch of black pepper in this warming, anti-inflammatory folk tincture. A drop of bottled sunlight for stiff mornings and aching joints.

ingredients.item: Turmeric root, fresh, grated (or 1/3 cup dried)
Ginger root, fresh, grated (or 3 tbsp dried)
Vodka, 100 proof (50% alcohol); use 151-190 proof if using all fresh roots

steps: Cleanse a clean, dry pint (500 ml) glass jar with a pass of incense smoke or a whispered blessing, and hold your intention as you work.

Grate the fresh roots (wear gloves: turmeric stains everything golden), then pack them with the cracked pepper and peel into the jar. For fresh roots use roughly 1:2 weight-to-volume with high-proof alcohol; for dried use 1:5 with 50%.
Pour the alcohol over the herbs until fully covered by at least 1 inch (2.5 cm); poke out air bubbles with a chopstick and top up over the first days if the plant matter swells.
Cap tightly (line metal lids with baking parchment), label with herbs, menstruum and date, and shake while speaking the chant.
Store in a cool, dark cupboard for 4-6 weeks, shaking daily; traditionally begin on a Sunday at the new moon and strain on the full moon, the sun's light at its fullest reflection.
Strain through a cheesecloth-lined strainer, squeezing the marc (spent herbs) firmly to release every drop, then return the herbs to the earth with thanks.
Bottle in amber dropper bottles and label with name, herbs, alcohol %, date made and dose. Stored cool and dark, alcohol tinctures keep for several years.
howToUse: Traditional adult dose: 30-60 drops (1.5-3 ml) in warm water, juice or milk 2-3 times daily with food, for no more than a few weeks at a time. Pepper and a little fat (warm milk, food) help the body take up turmeric.
chant: Golden root and fire root bright, warm my bones with healing light. Ease the ache and loose the stiff, sun within me, this my gift.
intention: I welcome warmth, ease and golden vitality into my body.
timing: New moon on a Sunday; strain at the full moon.
caution: Turmeric and ginger may thin the blood: avoid with anticoagulants or antiplatelet drugs (warfarin, aspirin, clopidogrel) and stop 2 weeks before surgery. Avoid with gallstones, bile duct obstruction or stomach ulcers. Turmeric in medicinal amounts is best avoided in pregnancy. May lower blood sugar and interact with diabetes medication. Can cause heartburn in large doses. Turmeric is the most common herbal cause of liver injury reported in the US, especially when combined with black pepper (piperine); stop and seek care for yellowing skin or eyes, dark urine, nausea or unusual tiredness, and avoid with liver disease. People prone to kidney stones or with iron deficiency should ask a doctor first. Alcohol-based: not for pregnancy, breastfeeding, children, anyone in recovery from alcohol use or avoiding alcohol, or people with liver disease, and never take it with disulfiram (Antabuse), metronidazole or tinidazole (or within 3 days of the last dose), or alongside sedatives, opioids or other medicines that react with alcohol. Stirring drops into hot water drives off only part of the alcohol, so it is never alcohol-free; a glycerite (3 parts food-grade glycerin to 1 part water) or vinegar version is the alcohol-free alternative. Traditional folk use only, not a substitute for medical care; consult a healthcare provider before use, especially if you take medication or have a health condition.
bestTime: Late autumn into winter, Samhain to Yule (Nov–Dec), when fresh roots are in season and cold settles into the joints
interactions: May add to warfarin, aspirin, clopidogrel and other blood thinners and to diabetes medicines; turmeric and black pepper can raise blood levels of some drugs (CYP3A4 substrates such as tacrolimus).
pets: Keep away from pets: alcohol tinctures are poisonous to dogs and especially cats.

name: Linden Blossom Heart-Ease Tincture
description: Linden (lime) trees were sacred to Freya and planted at the heart of Germanic villages where justice was spoken and lovers met. Its honey-sweet blossoms make a gentle, softening tincture for tension, a heavy heart and the nervous flutter of a busy mind.
steps: Cleanse a clean, dry pint (500 ml) glass jar with a pass of incense smoke or a whispered blessing, and hold your intention as you work.
Place the dried herbs in the jar, filling it about one-third to one-half full (roughly 1:5 weight-to-volume: 1 part dried herb by weight to 5 parts liquid by volume).
Pour the 80 proof (40%) vodka over the herbs until fully covered by at least 1 inch (2.5 cm); poke out air bubbles with a chopstick and top up over the first days if the plant matter swells.
Cap tightly (line metal lids with baking parchment), label with herbs, menstruum and date, and shake while speaking the chant.
Store in a cool, dark cupboard for 4-6 weeks, shaking daily; traditionally begin on a Friday at the new moon and strain at the full moon.
Strain through a cheesecloth-lined strainer, squeezing the marc (spent herbs) firmly to release every drop, then return the herbs to the earth with thanks.
Bottle in amber dropper bottles and label with name, herbs, alcohol %, date made and dose. Stored cool and dark, alcohol tinctures keep for several years.
howToUse: Traditional adult dose: 30-60 drops (1.5-3 ml) in warm water up to 3 times daily, or a dose before bed for gentle relaxation. Lovely added to a cup of linden tea at the end of the day.
chant: Linden blossom, Freya's tree, soften all that troubles me. Sweeten heart and still the mind, leave all tension far behind.
intention: My heart is soft, open and at ease.
timing: New moon on a Friday; strain at the full moon.
caution: Generally gentle. Rarely causes allergic reactions; avoid if allergic to linden. Traditionally avoided by people with heart conditions in large or frequent doses, so take care alongside heart or blood pressure medication. May add to the effect of sedatives. Alcohol-based: not for pregnancy, breastfeeding, children, anyone in recovery from alcohol use or avoiding alcohol, or people with liver disease, and never take it with disulfiram (Antabuse), metronidazole or tinidazole (or within 3 days of the last dose), or alongside sedatives, opioids or other medicines that react with alcohol. Stirring drops into hot water drives off only part of the alcohol, so it is never alcohol-free; a glycerite (3 parts food-grade glycerin to 1 part water) or vinegar version is the alcohol-free alternative. Traditional folk use only, not a substitute for medical care; consult a healthcare provider before use, especially if you take medication or have a health condition.
bestTime: Midsummer, around Litha (late Jun–Jul), when linden trees hum with bees
interactions: May add to sedatives; take care with heart and blood pressure medication and diuretics.
pets: Keep away from pets: alcohol tinctures are poisonous to dogs and especially cats.

name: Gladdening Lemon Balm Glycerite
description: Paracelsus called lemon balm the 'elixir of life', and medieval Carmelite nuns made it into a famous cordial for melancholy. This alcohol-free glycerite captures its lemony gladness in a sweet, child-friendly form for worries, sulks and unsettled tummies.

ingredients.item: Lemon Balm leaves, dried (or fresh, wilted overnight)
ingredients.amount: about 1 cup dried, or 2 cups fresh

steps: Cleanse a clean, sterilised pint (500 ml) glass jar and set your intention as you work.
Mix the menstruum first: 3 parts food-grade vegetable glycerin to 1 part distilled water (75% glycerin), stirring until smooth.
Place the dried lemon balm in the jar at about 1:5 weight-to-volume. If using fresh leaves, wilt them overnight to drive off some water and fill the jar loosely to the top.
Pour the glycerin mixture over the herbs to cover by at least 1 inch (2.5 cm), stir out air bubbles with a clean spoon and cap tightly.
Label and steep in a warm, dark place for 4-6 weeks, turning the jar daily; traditionally begin on a Monday at the new moon and strain at the full moon.
Strain through cheesecloth, squeezing the marc slowly (glycerites are thick and drain patiently), and compost the herbs with thanks.
Bottle in clean amber dropper bottles labelled with name, herbs, '75% glycerin, alcohol-free', date and dose. Refrigerate after opening.
howToUse: Traditional adult dose: 1/2-1 tsp (2.5-5 ml) or 40-60 drops in water up to 3 times daily. For children, give only glycerites at reduced doses (roughly one-quarter of the adult dose for ages 2-6, one-half for ages 7-12), never to infants under 1 year without professional advice. Can be taken straight from the spoon; it tastes like lemon honey.
chant: Balm of bees and gladdening green, wash away what's dark and mean. Sweet as honey, bright as sun, sorrow's spell is now undone.
intention: Gladness and gentle calm return to me and to my home.
timing: New moon on a Monday or Wednesday; strain at the full moon.
caution: Lemon balm may affect thyroid function; avoid with hypothyroidism or thyroid medication unless advised. May add to the effect of sedatives. Not for infants under 1 year. Glycerite (alcohol-free): glycerin is sweet and may loosen the bowels in large amounts; people with diabetes should count it as a sweetener. Keep the glycerin at 60% or more of the liquid or it may spoil; discard if cloudy, fizzy or sour-smelling. Keeps about 1-2 years cool and dark. Traditional folk use only, not a substitute for medical care; consult a healthcare provider before use, especially if you take medication, are pregnant or breastfeeding, or have a health condition.
bestTime: Early summer, Beltane to Litha (May–Jun), before lemon balm flowers
interactions: May add to the effects of sedatives and alcohol; may interfere with thyroid hormone medication.
pets: Keep away from pets; do not dose animals with herbal remedies without a veterinarian's advice.

name: Elderflower & Nettle Hay Fever Tincture
description: Elder is the Elder Mother's tree, guarded by a spirit who must be asked before a single flower is taken. Her creamy summer blossoms, paired with nettle and a touch of peppermint, make a cooling folk tincture for streaming eyes and sneezy hay-fever days.
steps: Cleanse a clean, dry pint (500 ml) glass jar with a pass of incense smoke or a whispered blessing, and hold your intention as you work.
Ask the Elder Mother's permission before harvesting, and remove all green stems (only the flowers are used). Place the dried herbs in the jar at roughly 1:5 weight-to-volume.

Pour the 80-100 proof (40-50%) vodka or brandy over the herbs until fully covered by at least 1 inch (2.5 cm); poke out air bubbles with a chopstick and top up over the first days if the plant matter swells.
Cap tightly (line metal lids with baking parchment), label with herbs, menstruum and date, and shake while speaking the chant.
Store in a cool, dark cupboard for 4-6 weeks, shaking daily; traditionally begin on the new moon and strain on the full moon a cycle and a half later.
Strain through a cheesecloth-lined strainer, squeezing the marc (spent herbs) firmly to release every drop, then return the herbs to the earth with thanks.
Bottle in amber dropper bottles and label with name, herbs, alcohol %, date made and dose. Stored cool and dark, alcohol tinctures keep for several years.
howToUse: Traditional adult dose: 30-60 drops (1.5-3 ml) in water 2-3 times daily. Folk practice is to begin a few weeks before pollen season and continue through it.
chant: Elder Mother, flowers white, nettle's green and mint so bright, clear my breath and ease my eyes, let the summer pollen rise.
intention: I breathe freely and welcome the green season with ease.
timing: New moon on a Wednesday; strain at the full moon.
caution: Use only elder flowers; elder leaves, bark, roots, seeds and unripe or raw berries can be toxic. Avoid with allergy to elder or the honeysuckle family. Nettle is mildly diuretic and may lower blood sugar and blood pressure; take care with diuretics, lithium, diabetes or blood pressure medication. Peppermint may worsen reflux. Alcohol-based: not for pregnancy, breastfeeding, children, anyone in recovery from alcohol use or avoiding alcohol, or people with liver disease, and never take it with disulfiram (Antabuse), metronidazole or tinidazole (or within 3 days of the last dose), or alongside sedatives, opioids or other medicines that react with alcohol. Stirring drops into hot water drives off only part of the alcohol, so it is never alcohol-free; a glycerite (3 parts food-grade glycerin to 1 part water) or vinegar version is the alcohol-free alternative. Traditional folk use only, not a substitute for medical care; consult a healthcare provider before use, especially if you take medication or have a health condition.
bestTime: Early summer, Beltane to Litha (late May–Jun), when elder is in blossom; begin taking in early spring
interactions: Nettle and elder flower may add to diuretics, lithium, diabetes and blood pressure medicines; nettle leaf contains vitamin K and may affect warfarin.
pets: Keep away from pets: alcohol tinctures are poisonous to dogs and especially cats.

name: Burdock Root Clear Skin Tincture
description: Burdock's clinging burrs inspired Velcro and its roots have long been dug as a 'blood cleanser' in European, Chinese and Japanese folk medicine. This earthy root tincture with red clover is a slow, deep alterative for troubled, inflamed skin.

ingredients.item: Burdock root, dried, chopped (or fresh first-year root)

steps: Cleanse a clean, dry pint (500 ml) glass jar with a pass of incense smoke or a whispered blessing, and hold your intention as you work.

If using fresh first-year burdock root (dug in autumn or early spring), scrub and chop it finely and use roughly 1:2 with high-proof alcohol; for dried roots and blossoms, place in the jar at 1:5 weight-to-volume.
Pour the alcohol over the herbs until fully covered by at least 1 inch (2.5 cm); poke out air bubbles with a chopstick and top up over the first days if the plant matter swells.
Cap tightly (line metal lids with baking parchment), label with herbs, menstruum and date, and shake while speaking the chant.
Store in a cool, dark cupboard for 4-6 weeks, shaking daily; traditionally begin just after the full moon and strain at the dark moon a cycle and a half later.
Strain through a cheesecloth-lined strainer, squeezing the marc (spent herbs) firmly to release every drop, then return the herbs to the earth with thanks.
Bottle in amber dropper bottles and label with name, herbs, alcohol %, date made and dose. Stored cool and dark, alcohol tinctures keep for several years.
howToUse: Traditional adult dose: 30-60 drops (1.5-3 ml) in water 2-3 times daily for at least 6-8 weeks, as alteratives work slowly. Drink plenty of water while taking it.
chant: Burdock deep in earthen bed, red clover blossom, sweet and red, draw out what is held within, clear and calm and heal my skin.
intention: I release what no longer serves me, inside and out.
timing: Waning moon on a Saturday; strain at the dark moon.
caution: Avoid with daisy-family allergy. Burdock and dandelion are diuretic and may lower blood sugar: take care with diuretics, lithium and diabetes medication. Red clover contains plant estrogens and may thin the blood: avoid with hormone-sensitive conditions, blood thinners and before surgery. Wild-harvesters must be certain of identification; young burdock leaves can be confused with toxic foxglove. Buy burdock root from a reputable supplier: commercial burdock root has been contaminated with belladonna (deadly nightshade), causing anticholinergic poisoning. Avoid in pregnancy (burdock may stimulate the uterus). Alcohol-based: not for pregnancy, breastfeeding, children, anyone in recovery from alcohol use or avoiding alcohol, or people with liver disease, and never take it with disulfiram (Antabuse), metronidazole or tinidazole (or within 3 days of the last dose), or alongside sedatives, opioids or other medicines that react with alcohol. Stirring drops into hot water drives off only part of the alcohol, so it is never alcohol-free; a glycerite (3 parts food-grade glycerin to 1 part water) or vinegar version is the alcohol-free alternative. Traditional folk use only, not a substitute for medical care; consult a healthcare provider before use, especially if you take medication or have a health condition.
bestTime: Autumn, Mabon to Samhain (Sep–Nov), when first-year roots are richest
interactions: May add to diuretics, lithium and diabetes medicines; red clover may add to blood thinners and interfere with hormone therapy, birth control and tamoxifen.
pets: Keep away from pets: alcohol tinctures are poisonous to dogs and especially cats.

name: Fresh Cleavers Spring Flow Tincture
description: Cleavers, also called goosegrass or sticky willy, clings to everything it touches and was once used by shepherds as a sieve for milk. Tinctured fresh in spring, it is a cooling, watery folk remedy to keep the lymph flowing and the body's waters moving.

ingredients.amount: enough to loosely fill a pint jar (about 3 cups)

ingredients.item: Grain alcohol, 151-190 proof (75-95%), or 100 proof vodka if not available
ingredients.amount: about 1 cup (250 ml), enough to cover

steps: Cleanse a clean, dry pint (500 ml) glass jar with a pass of incense smoke or a whispered blessing, and hold your intention as you work.
Gather cleavers in spring before seeds form, shake off insects, and chop finely. Fill the jar loosely to the top with fresh herb (the folk method for fresh plants, roughly 1:2 weight-to-volume).
Pour the high-proof grain alcohol over the herbs until fully covered by at least 1 inch (2.5 cm); poke out air bubbles with a chopstick and top up over the first days if the plant matter swells.
Cap tightly (line metal lids with baking parchment), label with herbs, menstruum and date, and shake while speaking the chant.
Store in a cool, dark cupboard for 4-6 weeks, shaking daily; traditionally begin on the waxing crescent of spring and strain at the full moon.

Strain through a cheesecloth-lined strainer, squeezing the marc (spent herbs) firmly to release every drop, then return the herbs to the earth with thanks. Fresh cleavers tincture is best used within 1-2 years, as it loses potency faster than dried-herb tinctures.
Bottle in amber dropper bottles and label with name, herbs, alcohol %, date made and dose. Stored cool and dark, alcohol tinctures keep for several years.
howToUse: Traditional adult dose: 30-60 drops (1.5-3 ml) in a glass of water 2-3 times daily for 2-4 weeks, especially in spring. Many herbalists also make a cold-water infusion of fresh cleavers to drink alongside.
chant: Cleaving green and clinging vine, cleanse these waters, keep them fine. Flow like river, flow like rain, wash me fresh and clear again.
intention: I let my waters flow clear, cool and renewed.
timing: Waxing crescent moon in spring, on a Monday; strain at the full moon.
caution: Cleavers is diuretic; take care with diuretic or lithium medication and with diabetes. Its hooked hairs may irritate sensitive skin when harvesting. Swollen lymph nodes that persist need medical assessment. Alcohol-based: not for pregnancy, breastfeeding, children, anyone in recovery from alcohol use or avoiding alcohol, or people with liver disease, and never take it with disulfiram (Antabuse), metronidazole or tinidazole (or within 3 days of the last dose), or alongside sedatives, opioids or other medicines that react with alcohol. Stirring drops into hot water drives off only part of the alcohol, so it is never alcohol-free; a glycerite (3 parts food-grade glycerin to 1 part water) or vinegar version is the alcohol-free alternative. Traditional folk use only, not a substitute for medical care; consult a healthcare provider before use, especially if you take medication or have a health condition.
bestTime: Early spring, Imbolc to Ostara (Mar–Apr), before cleavers goes to seed
interactions: May add to diuretics and lithium; take care with diabetes medicines.
pets: Keep away from pets: alcohol tinctures are poisonous to dogs and especially cats.

name: Chickweed Cooling Itch Liniment (External)
description: Humble chickweed carpets cool, shady ground and was fed to hens and caged songbirds, giving it the name 'starweed' for its tiny white flowers. Tinctured fresh, it becomes a cooling external liniment dabbed on itchy, irritated skin. For external use only.

ingredients.amount: enough to loosely fill a pint jar (about 3 cups)

ingredients.item: Grain alcohol 151-190 proof (75-95%), or 100 proof vodka
ingredients.amount: about 1 cup (250 ml), enough to cover

steps: Cleanse a clean, dry pint (500 ml) glass jar with a pass of incense smoke or a whispered blessing, and hold your intention as you work.
Harvest lush chickweed in cool weather, rinse and pat dry, chop finely with the plantain and fill the jar loosely to the top (folk method for fresh herbs, about 1:2).
Pour the high-proof alcohol over the herbs until fully covered by at least 1 inch (2.5 cm); poke out air bubbles with a chopstick and top up over the first days if the plant matter swells.
Cap tightly (line metal lids with baking parchment), label with herbs, menstruum and date, and shake while speaking the chant.
Store in a cool, dark cupboard for 4-6 weeks, shaking daily; traditionally begin at the full moon and strain at the following new moon, letting the waning draw the itch away.
Strain through a cheesecloth-lined strainer, squeezing the marc (spent herbs) firmly to release every drop, then return the herbs to the earth with thanks. Label clearly 'EXTERNAL USE ONLY'.

howToUse: EXTERNAL USE ONLY. Dilute 1 part liniment with 1-2 parts cool water or witch hazel and dab onto itchy, unbroken skin, bug bites and heat rash with a cotton pad 2-4 times daily. For a soothing compress, soak a cloth in the diluted liniment and lay it on the skin for 10 minutes.
chant: Starweed small and starweed cool, soothe this skin as moon soothes pool. Itch and burn and redness flee, cool and calm, so mote it be.
intention: I cool and calm all that burns and itches.
timing: Full moon on a Monday; strain at the new moon.
caution: EXTERNAL USE ONLY: this is high-proof alcohol; never swallow it, and label it clearly so it is not mistaken for an internal tincture. Alcohol stings and dries: do not apply to open wounds, burns, broken skin, near the eyes or on mucous membranes; patch test on the inner arm 24 hours first. Not for use on infants. Traditional folk use only, not a substitute for medical care; consult a healthcare provider before use, especially if you take medication, are pregnant or breastfeeding, or have a health condition.
bestTime: Early spring or autumn (Mar–Apr, Oct–Nov), when chickweed grows lush in cool weather
pets: Keep away from pets, who may lick treated skin or spills: high-proof alcohol is poisonous to dogs and especially cats.

name: Self-Heal All-Heal Tincture
description: Self-heal, also called heal-all and carpenter's herb, was so trusted by medieval folk that its name promised a person could heal themselves with it. Its purple-hooded flowers make a gently astringent tincture for sore throats, mouth sores and a world-weary spirit.

name: Passionflower Quiet Mind Simple

name: Catnip & Fennel Little Kitten Tummy Glycerite

chant: Kitten's mint and fennel sweet, settle tummy, warm the feet. Chamomile with golden eye, soothe the hurt and hush the cry.

description: The Anglo-Saxons believed wood betony protected against 'monstrous nocturnal visitors' and a medieval proverb advised, 'Sell your coat and buy betony.' This bittersweet tincture is a traditional remedy for tension headaches that come from a tight neck and an over-full head.

name: Feverfew Little Sun Migraine Tincture
description: Feverfew's daisy-like flowers have long been planted around homes to ward off sickness, and English cottagers ate a leaf a day in bread to keep away the 'megrim'. This bitter tincture is a traditional preventative for people prone to migraines, taken daily rather than in the moment.

description: Licorice root was found in Tutankhamun's tomb and was carried by Scythian warriors who could reportedly go days without water by chewing it. Traditional folk use only, not a substitute for medical care; consult a healthcare provider before use, especially if you take medication, are pregnant or breastfeeding, or have a health condition.
bestTime: Early summer, Beltane to Litha (May–Jun), when roses are in full bloom
interactions: Hawthorn may raise digoxin levels and intensify beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, nitrates and other blood pressure medicines, and may add to the effect of anticoagulants and antiplatelet drugs.
pets: Keep away from pets; do not dose animals with herbal remedies without a veterinarian's advice.

name: Oregano & Garlic Hedge Shield Tincture
description: Oregano, the 'joy of the mountain', was woven into Greek wedding crowns, while garlic has guarded doorways against vampires, plague and envy for millennia. Together with thyme, this pungent, warming tincture is a hedge-witch's first line of defence when colds and winter bugs come calling.
steps: Cleanse a clean, dry pint (500 ml) glass jar with a pass of incense smoke or a whispered blessing, and hold your intention as you work.
Chop the garlic and let it sit 10 minutes to develop its strength, then place it in the jar with the oregano, thyme and lemon peel at roughly 1:5 weight-to-volume.
Pour the 100 proof (50%) vodka over the herbs until fully covered by at least 1 inch (2.5 cm); poke out air bubbles with a chopstick and top up over the first days if the plant matter swells.
Cap tightly (line metal lids with baking parchment), label with herbs, menstruum and date, and shake while speaking the chant.
Store in a cool, dark cupboard for 4-6 weeks, shaking daily; traditionally begin on a Tuesday at the new moon (Mars day, for defence) and strain at the full moon.
Strain through a cheesecloth-lined strainer, squeezing the marc (spent herbs) firmly to release every drop, then return the herbs to the earth with thanks.
Bottle in amber dropper bottles and label with name, herbs, alcohol %, date made and dose. Stored cool and dark, alcohol tinctures keep for several years.
howToUse: Traditional adult dose: 20-40 drops (1-2 ml) in warm water or tea with honey 3 times daily at the first sign of a cold, for up to 7-10 days. Pungent: chase with something sweet. Diluted in warm water, it can also be gargled.
chant: Mountain joy and garlic white, thyme of courage, guard me tight. Bar the door to cold and ill, strong my shield and strong my will.
intention: My body is shielded, strong and well-defended.
timing: New moon on a Tuesday; strain at the full moon.
caution: Garlic may thin the blood: avoid with anticoagulants or antiplatelet drugs and stop 2 weeks before surgery. Garlic can reduce the effect of some HIV medicines (e.g. saquinavir) and other drugs. Oregano and thyme in medicinal amounts are best avoided in pregnancy and may trigger allergy in those sensitive to the mint family. May upset a sensitive stomach; take with food. Alcohol-based: not for pregnancy, breastfeeding, children, anyone in recovery from alcohol use or avoiding alcohol, or people with liver disease, and never take it with disulfiram (Antabuse), metronidazole or tinidazole (or within 3 days of the last dose), or alongside sedatives, opioids or other medicines that react with alcohol. Stirring drops into hot water drives off only part of the alcohol, so it is never alcohol-free; a glycerite (3 parts food-grade glycerin to 1 part water) or vinegar version is the alcohol-free alternative. Traditional folk use only, not a substitute for medical care; consult a healthcare provider before use, especially if you take medication or have a health condition.
bestTime: Autumn into winter, Mabon to Yule (Sep–Dec), ahead of cold and flu season
interactions: Garlic adds to warfarin and other blood thinners and antiplatelet drugs and can lower levels of HIV drugs such as saquinavir; oregano may add to diabetes medicines.
pets: Keep away from pets: garlic is poisonous to dogs, cats and horses (it damages red blood cells), and alcohol is poisonous to dogs and especially cats.

name: Angelica Root Archangel Digestive Tincture
description: Legend says the Archangel Michael revealed angelica to a monk as a cure for the plague, and it blooms around his feast day in some calendars. This aromatic, warming root tincture is a traditional bitter for sluggish digestion, wind and cold, heavy stomachs.
steps: Cleanse a clean, dry pint (500 ml) glass jar with a pass of incense smoke or a whispered blessing, and hold your intention as you work.
Buy angelica root from a reputable supplier rather than wild-harvesting (see caution). Place it with the crushed seeds, peel and cardamom in the jar at roughly 1:5 weight-to-volume.

Pour the 100 proof (50%) vodka or brandy over the herbs until fully covered by at least 1 inch (2.5 cm); poke out air bubbles with a chopstick and top up over the first days if the plant matter swells.
Cap tightly (line metal lids with baking parchment), label with herbs, menstruum and date, and shake while speaking the chant.
Store in a cool, dark cupboard for 4-6 weeks, shaking daily; traditionally begin on a Sunday at the new moon and strain at the full moon.
Strain through a cheesecloth-lined strainer, squeezing the marc (spent herbs) firmly to release every drop, then return the herbs to the earth with thanks.
Bottle in amber dropper bottles and label with name, herbs, alcohol %, date made and dose. Stored cool and dark, alcohol tinctures keep for several years.
howToUse: Traditional adult dose: 15-30 drops (0.75-1.5 ml) in a little water 10-15 minutes before meals, up to 3 times daily. Taste it on the tongue first: the bitter-aromatic flavour itself helps wake digestion.
chant: Angel's root of Michael's might, warm my belly, set it right. Fire within and wind be still, guard and guide me by your will.
intention: I am warmed, protected and well-nourished, guarded by angelic light.
timing: New moon on a Sunday; strain at the full moon.
caution: Do NOT wild-harvest angelica: it closely resembles deadly water hemlock and poison hemlock. Avoid in pregnancy (it stimulates the uterus) and breastfeeding. Angelica can cause photosensitivity: avoid strong sun or sunbeds while taking it. May thin the blood; avoid with anticoagulants and before surgery. Avoid with diabetes medication unless advised, and with stomach ulcers. Alcohol-based: not for pregnancy, breastfeeding, children, anyone in recovery from alcohol use or avoiding alcohol, or people with liver disease, and never take it with disulfiram (Antabuse), metronidazole or tinidazole (or within 3 days of the last dose), or alongside sedatives, opioids or other medicines that react with alcohol. Stirring drops into hot water drives off only part of the alcohol, so it is never alcohol-free; a glycerite (3 parts food-grade glycerin to 1 part water) or vinegar version is the alcohol-free alternative. Traditional folk use only, not a substitute for medical care; consult a healthcare provider before use, especially if you take medication or have a health condition.
bestTime: Autumn, Mabon to Samhain (Sep–Oct), when angelica roots are dug in their second year
interactions: May add to warfarin and other blood thinners and to diabetes medicines; may increase sun sensitivity with photosensitizing drugs; fennel may reduce ciprofloxacin absorption.
pets: Keep away from pets: alcohol tinctures are poisonous to dogs and especially cats.

name: Raspberry Leaf & Lady's Mantle Moon-Time Tincture
description: Raspberry leaf has been the 'woman's herb' of European and Indigenous American midwives for generations, toning the womb and easing the monthly cycle. Paired with Lady's Mantle, whose dew-cupped leaves alchemists gathered for the Philosopher's Stone, it is a gentle astringent ally for moon-time cramps.
steps: Cleanse a clean, dry pint (500 ml) glass jar with a pass of incense smoke or a whispered blessing, and hold your intention as you work.
Place the dried herbs in the jar, filling it about one-third to one-half full (roughly 1:5 weight-to-volume: 1 part dried herb by weight to 5 parts liquid by volume).

Pour the 80-100 proof (40-50%) vodka or brandy over the herbs until fully covered by at least 1 inch (2.5 cm); poke out air bubbles with a chopstick and top up over the first days if the plant matter swells.
Cap tightly (line metal lids with baking parchment), label with herbs, menstruum and date, and shake while speaking the chant.
Store in a cool, dark cupboard for 4-6 weeks, shaking daily; traditionally begin on a Monday at the new moon and strain at the full moon, honouring the lunar cycle that mirrors the menstrual one.
Strain through a cheesecloth-lined strainer, squeezing the marc (spent herbs) firmly to release every drop, then return the herbs to the earth with thanks.
Bottle in amber dropper bottles and label with name, herbs, alcohol %, date made and dose. Stored cool and dark, alcohol tinctures keep for several years.
howToUse: Traditional adult dose (when not pregnant): 30-60 drops (1.5-3 ml) in warm water 2-3 times daily, starting a few days before the expected period and through the first days of bleeding. Raspberry leaf tea is a gentle everyday alternative.
chant: Bramble leaf and Lady's cloak, ease the cramp and lift the yoke. Moon within and moon above, flow in balance, flow in love.
intention: I honour my cycle and move through it with ease and strength.
timing: New moon on a Monday; strain at the full moon.
caution: PREGNANCY: do NOT use this tincture in pregnancy. Raspberry leaf is traditionally used only in the final weeks of pregnancy, as a tea, and only under the guidance of a midwife or doctor; Lady's Mantle and alcohol must be avoided in pregnancy. Not for breastfeeding. Raspberry leaf may lower blood sugar; take care with diabetes medication. Heavy, very painful or irregular periods, or bleeding between periods, need medical assessment (e.g. for endometriosis or fibroids). Alcohol-based: not for pregnancy, breastfeeding, children, anyone in recovery from alcohol use or avoiding alcohol, or people with liver disease, and never take it with disulfiram (Antabuse), metronidazole or tinidazole (or within 3 days of the last dose), or alongside sedatives, opioids or other medicines that react with alcohol. Stirring drops into hot water drives off only part of the alcohol, so it is never alcohol-free; a glycerite (3 parts food-grade glycerin to 1 part water) or vinegar version is the alcohol-free alternative. Traditional folk use only, not a substitute for medical care; consult a healthcare provider before use, especially if you take medication or have a health condition.
bestTime: Early summer, Beltane to Litha (May–Jul), before the canes fruit and while Lady's Mantle is lush
interactions: Raspberry leaf may add to diabetes medicines; ginger may add to blood thinners.
pets: Keep away from pets: alcohol tinctures are poisonous to dogs and especially cats.

name: Lavender & Chamomile Moonlit Sleep Vinegar
description: Before distilled alcohol was common, herbal vinegars or 'aceta' were a staple of the still-room, and lavender vinegar was dabbed on the temples of fainting ladies. This alcohol-free vinegar tincture of lavender, chamomile and lemon balm is a gentle bedtime sip and a cooling headache compress.

ingredients.item: Raw apple cider vinegar (5% acidity), unpasteurised

steps: Cleanse a clean, dry quart (1 litre) glass jar and set your intention as you work.
Place the dried herbs in the jar, filling it about one-third full (roughly 1:5 weight-to-volume).
Pour the raw apple cider vinegar over the herbs until covered by at least 1 inch (2.5 cm), pressing everything down with a wooden spoon.
Cover the mouth with baking parchment before screwing on the lid (or use a plastic lid), label with contents and date, and shake while speaking the chant.
Steep in a cool, dark cupboard for 4-6 weeks, shaking daily; traditionally begin at the full moon and strain at the following dark moon, as the waning tide draws the day's cares away.
Strain through cheesecloth, pressing the herbs well, and compost them with thanks. If you like, stir in up to 1 part honey to 3 parts vinegar to make a sweet oxymel.
Bottle in glass with a non-metal cap, label with name, date and dose, and store in the refrigerator.
howToUse: Adult dose: 1-2 tsp (5-10 ml) in a cup of warm water (with honey if desired) 30-60 minutes before bed. For a tension headache, dilute 1 tbsp in a bowl of cool water, soak a cloth and lay it across the forehead. For children, give this vinegar diluted in water at reduced doses (roughly one-quarter of the adult dose for ages 2-6, one-half for ages 7-12), never to infants under 1 year without professional advice. (Honey-sweetened versions are never for babies under 1.)
chant: Lavender blue and moonlight pale, chamomile gold, let sleep prevail. Sour and sweet, the day is through, dreams of peace I call to you.
intention: I drift gently into peaceful, restoring sleep.
timing: Full moon on a Monday night; strain at the dark moon.
caution: Avoid with daisy-family allergy (chamomile). Lemon balm may affect thyroid function; avoid with thyroid conditions or medication unless advised. May add to the effect of sedatives. Never give honey to babies under 1 year. Vinegar-based (alcohol-free): acidic, so always dilute, rinse the mouth afterward to protect tooth enamel, and avoid with stomach ulcers, severe reflux or on low-potassium medication without advice. Use a plastic or parchment-lined lid, as vinegar corrodes metal. Keeps 6-12 months refrigerated. Traditional folk use only, not a substitute for medical care; consult a healthcare provider before use, especially if you take medication, are pregnant or breastfeeding, or have a health condition.
bestTime: Midsummer, Litha to Lughnasadh (Jun–Aug), when lavender and chamomile are harvested
interactions: May add to the effects of sedatives and alcohol; lemon balm may affect thyroid medication; vinegar may lower potassium with diuretics, digoxin or insulin.
pets: Keep away from pets; do not dose animals with herbal remedies without a veterinarian's advice.

name: Fire Cider Dragon's Breath Vinegar
description: Fire cider is a folk tonic popularised by herbalist Rosemary Gladstar in the 1970s, descended from much older four-thieves vinegars and cottage cold remedies. Fiery with garden staples of garlic, ginger, onion and cayenne, it is taken by the spoonful through the dark months to keep the inner fire burning.

ingredients.item: Turmeric root, fresh, grated (or 1 tbsp dried)
Cayenne pepper (fresh chili, sliced, or dried flakes)
Raw apple cider vinegar (5% acidity), unpasteurised
ingredients.amount: about 3-4 cups (750 ml-1 litre), to cover

steps: Cleanse a clean, dry quart (1 litre) glass jar and set your intention as you work.
Chop, slice and grate all the plant ingredients (wear gloves for the chili and turmeric) and pack them into the jar, filling it about three-quarters full. Breathe in the fire as you work.
Pour the raw apple cider vinegar over the herbs until covered by at least 1 inch (2.5 cm), pressing everything down with a wooden spoon.
Cover the mouth with baking parchment before screwing on the lid (or use a plastic lid), label with contents and date, and shake while speaking the chant.
Steep in a cool, dark cupboard for 4-6 weeks, shaking daily; traditionally begin on a Tuesday at the new moon, or at Samhain, and strain at the full moon a cycle and a half later.
Strain through cheesecloth, pressing the herbs well, and compost them with thanks. Stir in the honey to taste, until it is hot, sweet and sour all at once.
Bottle in glass with a non-metal cap, label with name, date and dose, and store in the refrigerator.
howToUse: Adult dose: 1 tbsp (15 ml) daily as a winter tonic, or 1 tsp every 3-4 hours at the first sign of a cold. Take straight, diluted in warm water or tea, or use as a salad dressing and marinade. Children over 2: 1/2-1 tsp diluted in water, if they enjoy it.
chant: Garlic, ginger, onion, flame, lemon bright, I speak your name. Burn the chill and clear the head, fire within, all sickness fled.
intention: My inner fire burns bright, warm and strong through the dark of the year.
timing: New moon on a Tuesday, or at Samhain; strain at the full moon.
caution: Very spicy: avoid with stomach ulcers, gastritis, severe reflux or irritable bowel. Garlic, ginger and turmeric may thin the blood; take care with anticoagulants and stop 2 weeks before surgery. Turmeric in large amounts is best avoided in pregnancy, with gallstones and with liver disease (rare liver injury has been reported, especially with black pepper). Avoid touching eyes after handling chili. Never give honey to babies under 1 year. Vinegar-based (alcohol-free): acidic, so always dilute, rinse the mouth afterward to protect tooth enamel, and avoid with stomach ulcers, severe reflux or on low-potassium medication without advice. Use a plastic or parchment-lined lid, as vinegar corrodes metal. Keeps 6-12 months refrigerated. Traditional folk use only, not a substitute for medical care; consult a healthcare provider before use, especially if you take medication, are pregnant or breastfeeding, or have a health condition.
bestTime: Autumn, Mabon to Samhain (Sep–Nov), to be ready for winter
interactions: Garlic, ginger and turmeric may add to warfarin and other blood thinners; garlic can lower levels of some HIV drugs; vinegar may lower potassium with diuretics, digoxin or insulin.
pets: Keep away from pets: garlic and onion are poisonous to dogs, cats and horses (they damage red blood cells).

name: Elecampane & Mullein Breath of the Elves Tincture
description: Elecampane was said to have sprung from Helen of Troy's tears and was sacred to the elves (hence 'elfwort'), while mullein's tall velvet spires were dipped in tallow as hag's tapers. Together they make a warming, expectorant tincture for wet, stubborn chest coughs that will not shift.

Place the dried herbs in the jar, filling it about one-third to one-half full (roughly 1:5 weight-to-volume: 1 part dried herb by weight to 5 parts liquid by volume).

timing: New moon on a Wednesday; strain at the full moon.
caution: Avoid with daisy-family allergy (elecampane). Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Elecampane may lower blood sugar and blood pressure and may add to the effect of sedatives; stop 2 weeks before surgery. Large doses may cause vomiting or diarrhea. Strain mullein carefully to remove hairs. Shortness of breath, chest pain, coughing blood, high fever, or a cough lasting more than 3 weeks needs medical care. Alcohol-based: not for pregnancy, breastfeeding, children, anyone in recovery from alcohol use or avoiding alcohol, or people with liver disease, and never take it with disulfiram (Antabuse), metronidazole or tinidazole (or within 3 days of the last dose), or alongside sedatives, opioids or other medicines that react with alcohol. Stirring drops into hot water drives off only part of the alcohol, so it is never alcohol-free; a glycerite (3 parts food-grade glycerin to 1 part water) or vinegar version is the alcohol-free alternative.
